notes.meaning: The writer calls on every person across the globe to stop and listen carefully. He invites people of all social standings, from powerful leaders to humble laborers, and both the wealthy and the poor. What he is about to share matters equally to all people because everyone must eventually face death.

The speaker promises to share true wisdom and deep understanding. He is not talking off the top of his head, but sharing truth that he has carefully weighed in his heart. His message provides practical guidance to help people live rightly before God.

The writer first listens humbly to the wise lessons God teaches before attempting to instruct others. He then sets this life lesson to music on the harp to help people remember it. Singing about hard questions helps untangle deep mysteries so ordinary listeners can grasp them.

Believers do not need to panic when difficult days arrive or when dishonest enemies try to trip them up. Those who attack God's people may seem powerful, but they are only dying mortals. Trusting in the Lord provides a deep calm even in the middle of danger.

Worldly people place their trust in money and brag about how much they own. They act as though their bank accounts can protect them from every trouble. Yet making wealth your security is foolish because money cannot protect anyone from life's greatest dangers.

No amount of money can buy back a person's life from the grave or pay a ransom to God. A wealthy man cannot bribe death to spare his own brother or dearest friend. God alone holds the authority over human life, and earthly treasure has no buying power in His courtroom.

A human life is far too precious to be bought with silver or gold. No earthly price could ever be high enough to keep someone alive forever and stop their body from decaying in the grave. Because money cannot buy eternal life, trusting in wealth to conquer death is completely hopeless.

Daily life proves that death comes for everyone without exception. Clever and educated people die just as surely as fools and thoughtless people perish. In the end, they all must leave their accumulated riches behind for others to use.

Deep down, proud people secretly imagine that their family empires and houses will endure forever. They even name their properties and estates after themselves so they will be remembered for generations. Yet these famous names cannot stop the grave from claiming them in the end.

No matter how much honor and fame a person earns, human life is short and cannot last. Earthly glory is like a guest that only stays for a single night before vanishing. Without God, even the most celebrated people die and decay just like the animals.

Placing full confidence in earthly success is plain foolishness. Even worse, each new generation tends to follow the same wrong path and repeat the same worldly sayings. People often fail to learn from the mistakes of their ancestors and keep chasing the same temporary prizes.

Like helpless sheep driven into a pen, the ungodly are led away with death as their shepherd. Their outward beauty and royal grandeur will rot away inside the dark tomb. But for believers, the morning of rising from the dead will dawn, and the faithful will be vindicated while the wicked are brought low.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars interpret 'the morning' not as the final resurrection, but as a metaphor for a sudden change of circumstances in this life or an allusion to morning court sessions.

notes.meaning: In direct contrast to the fate of the worldly, the psalmist knows God will rescue his soul from the power of the grave. The Lord will redeem him—meaning buy him back from death—and receive him into His presence. This confident hope looks beyond the grave to eternal fellowship with God.

Believers are warned not to feel upset or intimidated when ungodly people get rich. We should not be troubled when a neighbor's house grows in size, power, and prestige. Their material success is temporary and does not mean God is on their side.

When wealthy unbelievers die, they cannot take any of their possessions with them. They must leave behind every coin, house, and honor they spent their lives gathering. Earthly glory stops cold at the edge of the grave.

During his life, the rich man congratulated himself on his comfort, thinking he had achieved true happiness. Society regularly flatters and praises people who look out for themselves and make a great deal of money. Yet all that earthly approval means nothing if a person is spiritually bankrupt before God.

The self-satisfied rich person will eventually join the earlier generations of ancestors who have already died. Cut off from God's presence, they will never again see the light of life or joy. Their self-made celebration ends in permanent darkness.

A person who possesses great wealth and public honor but lacks spiritual understanding is no better off than a dying animal. It is true wisdom and relationship with God that elevate human beings above the rest of creation. Without that wisdom, all worldly greatness ends in tragic and everlasting ruin.
